newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Jewish groups tap members for Swiss Holocaust fund.
newsitem.headline: Jewish groups tap members for Swiss Holocaust fund.

text.p: Jewish groups have proposed author Elie Wiesel, U.S. official Stuart Eizenstat and Israeli member of parliament Avraham Hirschson be named directors of the Swiss Holocaust memorial fund, a Jewish leader said on Thursday.

Rolf Bloch, president of the Swiss Jewish Federation (SIG), said Jewish groups also suggested that he himself lead the fund's seven-member board of directors, whose members must still be approved by the government in Berne.
"The Swiss cabinet will take note of these suggestions and decide whom to elect after its holiday," Bloch told Reuters.

Wiesel is a Holocaust survivor and human rights campaigner. Eizenstat, U.S. undersecretary of commerce for international trade, is directing Washington's effort to comb its archives for records of Switzerland's financial dealings with the Nazis.
Hirschson is in charge of Holocaust survivors' affairs in Israel, Bloch said.
The Swiss government last month approved the memorial fund, which gives Jewish groups a big say in how to distribute million of dollars in humanitarian aid to Hitler's victims.

The move helped to defuse the country's worst foreign policy crisis since World War Two, sparked by allegations that Swiss banks hoarded unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims and that the neutral Switzerland cynically profited from the war.
Galvanised by international pressure and boycott threats, the three biggest Swiss banks launched the fund as a goodwill gesture with a 100 million franc ($68.7 million) donation.

The Swiss National Bank has also contributed 100 million francs to make amends for its wartime purchases of gold from Nazi Germany, much of it looted from the countries and people conquered by Hitler's legions.
Pledges from other banks and private businesses have brought the total to around 265 million francs.
The government maintains overall supervision of the fund, which aims to support needy Holocaust victims or others who were persecuted because of their race, religion or political views.
Officials have said a large part of the money is likely to go to Jewish groups and individuals in Eastern Europe who were cut off from compensation for decades by the Iron Curtain.

The decree sets up a board of seven directors, four of them Swiss to be named by Berne and three to be named by the World Jewish Restitution Organisation (WJRO), an umbrella group of major Jewish organisations and the state of Israel.
Bloch is tipped to lead the panel in order to strike a 50-50 balance between Jewish representatives and Swiss citizens.
The fund will have an advisory council of 18 members named by Swiss and foreign organisations including Jewish and other Holocaust victims, such as European gypsies.
It will recommend to the directors how to spend the money.

The fund is separate from a proposed seven billion Swiss franc Swiss Solidarity Foundation that would sell official gold reserves to finance aid to victims of poverty, catastrophes and human rights outrages, including the Holocaust.

Separately, the government task force coordinating the country's response to attacks on its wartime role as a financial centre with close links to the Nazis said it had turned to disseminate documents, speeches, photos and news releases. It can be found at http://www.eda-tf.ethz.ch.
